steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on SureFED, a peer-to-peer federated learning method that uses uncertainty quantification to stay robust against byzantine and poisoning attacks. It should cover why existing defenses fall short, the core idea of the method, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Federated learning: motivation and extensions
- Poisoning attacks and three categories of existing defenses
- How each defense category works
- Known weaknesses of existing defenses
- SureFED: two models per client, uncertainty-aware evaluation, introspection
- Inspiration from opinion dynamics; no benign majority needed
- Evaluation setup and summary of contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Federated learning: motivation and extensions
  - large networks, decentralized operation; clients hold local datasets
  - local data not enough for accurate global model; privacy blocks raw data sharing
  - federated learning algorithms, e.g. Federated Averaging
  - extensions: scalability in peer-to-peer setting, non-IID data
- Poisoning attacks and three categories of defenses
  - FL vulnerable to byzantine/adversarial attacks: data and model poisoning
  - (1) statistics-based: Trimmed Mean, Clipping
  - (2) model evaluation on local dataset: Zeno
  - (3) comparison with server's local model: FLTrust
- How each category works
  - statistics-based: robust quantity (median not mean) in aggregation; assumes benign majority
  - Zeno: samples from clean local dataset, scores update by loss improvement
  - FLTrust: bootstraps trust from server's local model; server has clean dataset, computes own update, compares
- Weaknesses
  - vulnerable to colluding "A Little is Enough" attacks and Trojan attacks
  - statistics-based need benign majority
  - Trimmed Mean, Zeno need upper bound on number of compromised clients
  - Zeno vulnerable to Trojan (stealthy)
  - FLTrust vulnerable to attacks on cosine-similarity methods; server model poisoned early -> later evaluations meaningless
- SureFED
  - uncertainty quantification; builds on existing defenses + extra components
  - peer-to-peer: local dataset + models from other clients
  - two models: social model (aggregates models from across network) and Local Bayesian Model (local data only, evaluation basis, explicit uncertainty)
  - local model never aggregated; Uncertainty Aware Model Evaluation, then new secure aggregation rule into social model
  - introspection: client checks own social model with clean local model -> can revert to clean state
- Opinion dynamics inspiration
  - bounded confidence models of opinion dynamics: how humans change opinions in interaction
  - emulate human intelligence in AI
  - each update evaluated independently, no comparison with other updates
  - => no benign majority, no knowledge of number of compromised clients
- Evaluation and contributions
  - six attacks: Label-Flipping, Trojan, Bit-Flip, General Random, A little is Enough, Gaussian
  - A little is Enough and Trojan colluding; Trojan also stealthy
  - baselines: Trimmed Mean, Clipping (cat. 1), Zeno (cat. 2), FLTrust (cat. 3), BayP2PFL (no defense, variational P2P FL)
  - theory: decentralized linear regression, non-IID; such guarantees rare
  - contributions: new robust P2P FL algorithm; properties (i)-(iii); proofs for Label-Flipping, generalized to General Random; experiments on MNIST, FEMNIST, CIFAR10 against all six attacks

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Today, in large networks, operations are decentralized and individual devices, which we call clients, have access to their own local datasets. But a local dataset is often not enough to learn a global model with good enough accuracy, and clients cannot just share their raw data with each other because of privacy concerns. Federated learning algorithms such as Federated Averaging were proposed to deal with these challenges. Many extensions were also introduced, either for better scalability in a peer-to-peer setting or to adapt to non-IID data distributions.

However, it has been shown that federated learning algorithms are vulnerable to different byzantine and adversarial attacks, for example data poisoning and model poisoning attacks. The state of the art defense methods in federated learning can be put into three categories. The first category is statistics-based defenses, such as Trimmed Mean and Clipping. The second category is defenses that evaluate the model on a local dataset, such as Zeno. The third category is defenses that compare the model with the server's local model, such as FLTrust.

The statistics-based defenses use a statistically robust quantity like the median instead of the mean when they aggregate the models, so that byzantine updates do not affect the aggregated value. These methods assume that most clients are benign, and the idea is that a statistical measure like the median is protected from being influenced by a minority of poisoned updates. Defenses in the second category, like Zeno, take samples from a clean local dataset and evaluate a model update based on how much it improves the loss function. Defenses in the third category, like FLTrust, bootstrap the trust by using the server's local model. FLTrust assumes the server has access to a clean local dataset. The server computes its own model update on this local dataset, in the same way the clients do, and then it compares the updates it receives with its own update.

It has been shown that the existing defense methods are vulnerable to specific attacks, such as the colluding attacks of "A Little is Enough" and Trojan attacks. Also, the statistics-based defenses need the majority of clients to be benign. Some methods, for example Trimmed Mean and Zeno, need to know an upper bound on how many clients are compromised. Zeno is also vulnerable to Trojan attacks by nature, because Trojan attacks are stealthy. FLTrust has also been shown to be vulnerable to specific attacks that target methods based on cosine similarity. Another possible drawback of FLTrust is that if the server's model gets poisoned early in the training, then all the model evaluations after that become meaningless.

- SureFED
  - uses uncertainty quantification, builds on existing defenses plus extra components
  - peer-to-peer: each client has local dataset, also receives models from others
  - two models: social model (aggregates models across network) and Local Bayesian Model (local data only, evaluation basis with explicit uncertainty)
  - local model never aggregated; Uncertainty Aware Model Evaluation then new secure aggregation rule
  - introspection: each client checks its own social model with its clean local model -> revert to clean state
- Opinion dynamics inspiration
  - bounded confidence models of opinion dynamics; how humans change opinions
  - each update evaluated independently -> no benign majority, no knowledge of number of compromised clients
- Evaluation and contributions
  - six attacks: Label-Flipping, Trojan, Bit-Flip, General Random, A little is Enough, Gaussian; A little is Enough and Trojan colluding, Trojan stealthy
  - baselines: Trimmed Mean, Clipping, Zeno, FLTrust, BayP2PFL (no defense)
  - theory: decentralized linear regression, non-IID; rare in literature
  - contributions list: algorithm; properties (i)-(iii); proofs (Label-Flipping, then General Random); MNIST, FEMNIST, CIFAR10 experiments vs all six attacks

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Today, in large networks, operations are decentralized and individual devices, which we call clients, have access to their own local datasets. But a local dataset is often not enough to learn a global model with good enough accuracy, and clients cannot just share their raw data with each other because of privacy concerns. Federated learning algorithms such as Federated Averaging were proposed to deal with these challenges. Many extensions were also introduced, either for better scalability in a peer-to-peer setting or to adapt to non-IID data distributions.

However, it has been shown that federated learning algorithms are vulnerable to different byzantine and adversarial attacks, for example data poisoning and model poisoning attacks. The state of the art defense methods in federated learning can be put into three categories. The first category is statistics-based defenses, such as Trimmed Mean and Clipping. The second category is defenses that evaluate the model on a local dataset, such as Zeno. The third category is defenses that compare the model with the server's local model, such as FLTrust.

The statistics-based defenses use a statistically robust quantity like the median instead of the mean when they aggregate the models, so that byzantine updates do not affect the aggregated value. These methods assume that most clients are benign, and the idea is that a statistical measure like the median is protected from being influenced by a minority of poisoned updates. Defenses in the second category, like Zeno, take samples from a clean local dataset and evaluate a model update based on how much it improves the loss function. Defenses in the third category, like FLTrust, bootstrap the trust by using the server's local model. FLTrust assumes the server has access to a clean local dataset. The server computes its own model update on this local dataset, in the same way the clients do, and then it compares the updates it receives with its own update.

It has been shown that the existing defense methods are vulnerable to specific attacks, such as the colluding attacks of "A Little is Enough" and Trojan attacks. Also, the statistics-based defenses need the majority of clients to be benign. Some methods, for example Trimmed Mean and Zeno, need to know an upper bound on how many clients are compromised. Zeno is also vulnerable to Trojan attacks by nature, because Trojan attacks are stealthy. FLTrust has also been shown to be vulnerable to specific attacks that target methods based on cosine similarity. Another possible drawback of FLTrust is that if the server's model gets poisoned early in the training, then all the model evaluations after that become meaningless.

In this paper we introduce SureFED, which uses uncertainty quantification to address these limitations of the existing literature. SureFED takes inspiration from the state of the art defense methods described above, and it adds some additional essential components to deal with the known vulnerabilities of those methods. SureFED uses a peer-to-peer federated learning setting where each client has a local dataset but also gets models from other clients. Unlike prior work, in SureFED the clients train two different models. The first one is a social model, which is meant to capture the benefits of federated operation by aggregating the models trained on the different datasets across the network. The second one is a Local Bayesian Model, which is trained only on the client's own local dataset and is used as the basis for evaluating models, with explicit uncertainty quantification. These local models are never aggregated with the received updates. Instead, they are used in an Uncertainty Aware Model Evaluation of the model updates, and then the updates are aggregated with the social model using a new secure aggregation rule. SureFED also has an introspection procedure, where each client evaluates its own social model using its clean local model. This makes sure the system can go back to a clean state after it was possibly contaminated.

The way SureFED evaluates and aggregates models is inspired by concepts from social science, such as bounded confidence models of opinion dynamics, which try to simulate how humans change their opinions when they interact with others. In this way, SureFED tries to emulate the innate intelligence of humans in the complex domain of AI. In SureFED, each received model update is evaluated independently and does not need to be compared with other updates. Because of this, SureFED works without needing a majority of benign clients and without knowing the number of compromised clients.

We investigate the performance of SureFED under a broad set of byzantine and adversarial attacks and show that it performs better. We consider six colluding and non-colluding data and model poisoning attacks, which are Label-Flipping, Trojan, Bit-Flip, General Random, A little is Enough, and Gaussian attacks. A little is Enough and Trojan are colluding attacks, and the Trojan attack is also a stealthy attack. We compare our results with the state of the art defense methods we described above. We compare SureFED with Trimmed Mean and Clipping from the first category, with Zeno, which is the state of the art in the second category, and with FLTrust, which is the state of the art in the third category. We also compare with BayP2PFL, which is a variational peer-to-peer federated learning baseline without any defense method, to confirm that the robustness of SureFED does not cost reliability and/or performance. Besides the experiments, we also give theoretical guarantees for the robustness of SureFED in a decentralized linear regression setting under non-IID data distribution. Theoretical guarantees in non-IID settings are rare in the literature. Our contributions are:

- We introduce SureFED, a new peer-to-peer federated learning algorithm that is robust to a variety of data and model poisoning attacks.

- SureFED has the following good properties: (i) its robustness does not need the benign nodes to be the majority over the compromised ones, and it is agnostic to the number of byzantine workers; (ii) it adapts to the non-IID datasets of benign clients and gets benefits from them; (iii) it is robust to many poisoning attacks and performs better than the state of the art defense methods.

- We prove the robustness of SureFED theoretically in a decentralized linear regression setting under certain poisoning attacks. We prove that the benign nodes in SureFED learn the correct model parameter under Label-Flipping attacks, and then we generalize the theoretical results to the General Random model poisoning attack.

- Proof-of-concept evaluations on benchmark data from image classification (MNIST, FEMNIST, and CIFAR10) show that SureFED is better than the existing defense methods, which are Zeno, Trimmed Mean, Clipping, and FLTrust. We evaluate the robustness for all six types of poisoning attacks.

steps.text:
In contemporary large networks, operations are decentralized and individual devices (clients) have access to their local datasets. However, these local datasets often lack the capacity to learn a global model with sufficient accuracy, and privacy concerns prevent clients from sharing raw data. To address these challenges, federated learning algorithms [1] such as Federated Averaging have been proposed. In addition, a number of extensions were introduced to improve scalability in a peer-to-peer setting or to adapt to non-IID data distributions [2,3,4,5,6,7].

However, federated learning algorithms have been shown to be vulnerable to various byzantine and adversarial attacks, including data and model poisoning attacks [8,9,10,11,12,13,14]. State of the art defense methods in federated learning fall into three categories: (1) statistics-based defenses [15,16,17,18,19], such as Trimmed Mean [15] and Clipping [20], (2) defenses based on evaluating the model on a local dataset [21,22], such as Zeno [21], and (3) defenses based on comparing the model with the server's local model, such as FLTrust [23].

Statistics-based defense methods use a statistically robust quantity, such as the median instead of the mean, in model aggregation to eliminate the effect of byzantine updates on the aggregated value. Such methods assume that the majority of clients are benign, so that statistical measures like the median are protected from being influenced by a minority of poisoned updates. Defenses in the second category, such as Zeno [21], draw samples from a clean local dataset and evaluate a model update based on how much it improves the loss function. Defenses in the third category, such as FLTrust [23], bootstrap trust using the server's local model. FLTrust assumes that the server has access to a clean local dataset; the server computes a model update on this dataset just as the clients do and compares the received updates with its own.

The existing defense methods have been shown to be vulnerable to specific attacks such as the colluding attacks of "A Little is Enough" [24] and Trojan attacks [25]. In addition, the statistics-based defenses require the majority of clients to be benign. Some methods, such as Trimmed Mean [15] and Zeno [21], require knowledge of an upper bound on the number of compromised clients. Zeno is also inherently vulnerable to Trojan attacks because of their stealthy nature. FLTrust has also been shown to be vulnerable to specific attacks targeting methods based on cosine similarity [26]. A further potential drawback of FLTrust is that if the server's model is poisoned early in training, all future model evaluations become meaningless.

This paper introduces SureFED, which uses uncertainty quantification to address these limitations in the existing literature. SureFED draws inspiration from the state of the art defense methods described above and adds further essential components to address their known vulnerabilities. SureFED uses a peer-to-peer federated learning setting in which each client has access to a local dataset but also obtains models from other clients. In contrast with prior work, the clients in SureFED train two distinct models: a social model, designed to capture the benefits of federated operation by aggregating the models trained on diverse datasets across the network, and a Local Bayesian Model, trained only on each client's local dataset and used as a basis for model evaluation with explicit uncertainty quantification. These local models are never aggregated with the received updates; instead, they are used in an Uncertainty Aware Model Evaluation of the model updates, which are then aggregated with the social model based on a new secure aggregation rule. SureFED also employs an introspection procedure, in which each client evaluates its own social model using its clean local model. This ensures that the system can revert to a clean state after potential contamination.

Model evaluation and aggregation in SureFED are inspired by concepts from social science such as bounded confidence models of opinion dynamics [27], which aim to simulate how humans change their opinions during interactions with others. In this sense, SureFED seeks to emulate the innate intelligence of humans within the complex domain of AI. Notably, each received model update in SureFED is evaluated independently, without comparison to other updates. This allows SureFED to function without a majority of benign clients and without knowledge of the number of compromised clients.

We investigate the performance of SureFED under a broad set of byzantine and adversarial attacks and demonstrate its superiority. In particular, we consider six colluding and non-colluding data and model poisoning attacks: Label-Flipping [10], Trojan [25], Bit-Flip [28], General Random [28], A little is Enough [24], and Gaussian [29] attacks. A little is Enough and Trojan are colluding attacks, and the Trojan attack is also stealthy. We compare our results with the state of the art defense methods described above: Trimmed Mean [15] and Clipping [20] from the first category, Zeno [21], the state of the art in the second category, and FLTrust [23], the state of the art in the third category. We also compare with BayP2PFL [6], a variational peer-to-peer federated learning baseline without a defense method, to confirm that SureFED's robustness does not come at the cost of reliability and/or performance. In addition to the experimental analysis, we provide theoretical guarantees for the robustness of SureFED in a decentralized linear regression setting under non-IID data distribution; such guarantees in non-IID settings are rarely found in the literature. In summary, our contributions are as follows:

- We introduce SureFED, a new peer-to-peer federated learning algorithm that is robust to a variety of data and model poisoning attacks.

- SureFED has the following desirable properties: (i) its robustness does not require benign nodes to outnumber compromised ones and is agnostic to the number of byzantine workers; (ii) SureFED adapts to and benefits from the non-IID datasets of benign clients; (iii) SureFED is robust to numerous poisoning attacks and outperforms the state of the art defense methods.

- We theoretically prove the robustness of SureFED in a decentralized linear regression setting under certain poisoning attacks. We prove that the benign nodes in SureFED learn the correct model parameter under Label-Flipping attacks, and then generalize our theoretical results to the General Random model poisoning attack.

- Comprehensive proof-of-concept evaluations on benchmark image classification data (MNIST, FEMNIST, and CIFAR10) demonstrate the superiority of SureFED over existing defense methods, namely Zeno, Trimmed Mean, Clipping, and FLTrust, with robustness evaluated against all six types of poisoning attacks.
